full_judgment:
15. Before I entering into the merit of the present case let us look into the provision of section 95 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (Briefly, SAT Act, 1950). Before the amendment made in the year 1969 by the Ordinance No. XX1 of 1969 in section 95 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act maximum period for a usufructuary mortgage was 15 years and by this amendment the same period was reduced to seven years. And unless earlier redeemed by repayment of the consideration a mortgagor acquires right to redemption on the expiry of the maximum period of seven years, and if the mortgagee does not voluntarily restore possession of the land to the mortgagor, the latter may file a suit for redemption within a period of 60 years from the date of accrual of his right of redemption under Article 147 of the Limitation Act. In the present case the suit was filed on 9-4-2006 after expiry of 35 years which is well within the period of limitation and same it is not barred by limitation. 

 16. Again section 95 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 has been amended by the President's Order No. 88 of 1972 with effect from 3-8-1972, but this amendment did not touch the period of a usufructuary mortgage which is still 7 (seven) years, nor did it affect the period of limitation for redemption suit which is 60 years. Thus it shows that firstly if, on the expiry of the period of a mortgage, the mortgagee does not restore possession of the land to the mortgagor, then the Sub-divisional Magistrate shall on an application by the mortgagor, restore possession of the mortgagor by evicting the mortgagee. In other words, for getting back possession of a mortgaged land the mortgagor need no file any redemption suit, but may get quick remedy by an application to the Sub-divisional Magistrate. The other provision in the amendment is that notwithstanding anything contained in any other law in force, any transfer of land by an out and out sale with a condition for reconveyance shall be deemed to be a complete usufructuary mortgage for a period not exceeding 7 (seven) years on the expiry of which the mortgagor may get back possession by an application to the Sub-divisional Magistrate. But since transfer as I have found a mortgage, no question arises whether it should be treated as mortgage. 

 19. Before parting with the case it may be mentioned that the learned judge of the appellate court took note of the case of Bangladesh vs Haji Abdul Gani Biswas, reported in 32 DLR (AD) 233. The reference of that case in the contention of the present case is wholly irrelevant. The historical background of the legislation is mentioned in PO No. 88 of 1972 in respect of subsisting usufractuary mortgage is hit by section 95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act which is meant to protect the helpless raiyat. A raiyat in Bangladesh cannot interfere into any form of usufractuary mortgage other than complete usufractuary mortgage which is capable of enjoyment for a maximum period of seven years and the raiyat will get back his property under section 95 of SAT Act, 1950.
